Faraz Rahman CS, Math and Robotics @ University of Pennsylvania

Decision Making Diffusion Models

(Note: this blog will temporarily serve as a summary of the main results, while I am still working on the write up)

Diffusion models (DMs) in their various forms have become extremely powerful tools to generatively sample from high-dimensional distributions. Originally DMs were designed to sample from the space of images, but more recent work have brought applications in sampling motion plans, biochemical structures and more. While there is rich theory going back to the (insert time) on the time-reversed Langevin process, most recent works abstract the away the diffusion trajectory and focus study on the quality of the generated sample leaving open questions about insight we might gain from studying diffusion trajectories.

This project aims to provide preliminary answers to two questions. The first naturally arises from the fact that diffusion is a time-variant process: given a set of features from a diffusion sample, which were generated earlier and which later? To answer this question we study the decline in variance over time of a DM output by conditioning on some prefix of a given diffusion trajectory.

We find that the variance of certain features drop significantly earlier than others in a couple of data sets suggesting that those features were generated first and can be thought of as a prior when generating later features.

The second question follows from the first. Can we use this above ordering to break down our diffusion trajectory into smaller piece wise linear components using system identification? If so, can techniques from control theory and linear systems provide insight into how features influence each other through the diffusion process? Our results here are more rudimentary, but we hope that it may provide useful intuition to a practitioner or inspire future work.

In asking these questions, we also generated a toy dataset of block bisections (see below) to test if diffusion trajectories could faithfully learn interdependencies encoded in how we generated the block data.

The general theme of the results here suggest that DMs partake is some form of reasoning as the forward process occurs. Further exposition of this idea will be available in a formal write up soon.
